  "Conceptual Assets": [
    {
      "Concept ID": "C1",
      "Concept Name": "Lock state",
      "Unit": "neorv32_hwspinlock",
      "Information": "The 32 per-entry lock states represent ownership and availability of the spinlock resources, on which software synchronization depends. The state is generated and stored internally with no entry port, and lock status leaves through the response data field.",
      "Rubric": {
        "Confidentiality": "no",
        "Integrity": "yes",
        "Availability": "yes",
        "Undermined Expected Behavior": "no"
      },
      "Rubric Reason": "An unchecked bus request can rewrite a lock bit through the strobe, address and read/write tests at lines 44-45, allowing unauthorized modification of synchronization state. An attacker can set lock bits through the same path and leave locks asserted, causing legitimate clients to spin and making the lock service unavailable at lines 44-45.",
      "Objectives At Risk": [
        "I",
        "A"
      ],
      "Attack": "An attacker can issue bus accesses that set or clear selected lock bits, breaking mutual exclusion or keeping resources permanently locked.",

        "bus_rsp_o.data"
      ],

        70
      ]
    },
    {
      "Concept ID": "C2",
      "Concept Name": "Lock-entry selection",
      "Unit": "neorv32_hwspinlock",
      "Information": "The lock-entry selection chooses which lock is updated and which per-entry lock status is returned, so accesses depend on it to target the intended resource. It is an internal address decode that only decides lock accesses and therefore has no direct entry or exit port.",
      "Rubric": {
        "Confidentiality": "no",
        "Integrity": "yes",

      "Objectives At Risk": [

conceptual assets.information: The 32 per-entry lock states represent ownership and availability of the spinlock resources, on which software synchronization depends. The state is generated and stored internally with no entry port, and lock status leaves through the response data field.
conceptual assets.rubric reason: An unchecked bus request can rewrite a lock bit through the strobe, address and read/write tests at lines 44-45, allowing unauthorized modification of synchronization state. An attacker can set lock bits through the same path and leave locks asserted, causing legitimate clients to spin and making the lock service unavailable at lines 44-45.
conceptual assets.attack: An attacker can issue bus accesses that set or clear selected lock bits, breaking mutual exclusion or keeping resources permanently locked.

conceptual assets.information: The lock-entry selection chooses which lock is updated and which per-entry lock status is returned, so accesses depend on it to target the intended resource. It is an internal address decode that only decides lock accesses and therefore has no direct entry or exit port.
conceptual assets.rubric reason: The selector is derived from the request address at line 51 and controls which lock bit is written through the condition at lines 44-45, so changing the address can steer a modification to the wrong entry. The selector can direct an acquisition or release away from the intended entry, withholding the required lock operation through the same gated assignment at lines 44-45.
conceptual assets.attack: An attacker can forge the request address so that an access modifies or observes a different lock entry than the one intended.

considered, not kept.reason: The strobe, read/write direction and ordinary access-address command are folded into the access under Access command fields; only the derived entry selector is kept separately, as shown by lines 44 and 66-67.

considered, not kept.concept: Bus response handshake and error status
considered, not kept.reason: The acknowledge repeats the request strobe and the error field is assigned a constant at lines 63-65, so they are only handshake or constant status and have no independent security asset.
Clock and reset inputs are explicitly excluded as conceptual assets because they only time or reset the lock and response state at lines 41-43 and 60-62.
